compatibility.title: Which Mercedes Models Use the M178.980?
compatibility.intro: The M178 is the exclusive powerplant for the Mercedes-AMG GT lineage (C190/C192). Unlike the wet-sump M177 found in AMG saloons and SUVs, the M178 features a dedicated dry-sump lubrication system to lower the engine's center of gravity and ensure consistent oil pickup under extreme lateral and longitudinal G-forces on the track.

costGuide.title: Mercedes-AMG M178 Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting an M178 engine typically takes 18-26 hours at £85-£110/hr (AMG specialist) - the dry-sump plumbing, tight mid-engine bay, and complex subframe removal make extraction highly labour-intensive.
paragraphs: What genuinely moves the price for this engine is the condition of the cylinder bores, the twin turbochargers, and the dry-sump oil reservoir and pump assembly. Because early M178 engines are prone to cylinder scoring under track use, reputable recon specialists will typically borescope the block, install Darton iron cylinder sleeves if scoring is present, and upgrade the hot-vee turbo oil feed lines to prevent immediate post-installation failures. For a full breakdown of market rates, see our full reconditioned engine cost guide.

failures.title: Mercedes-AMG M178 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Cylinder Wall Scoring (Alusil Block Wear)
items.whatHappens: The M178 features an Alusil (aluminum-silicon) coated cylinder block. Under high boost, immense thermal loads, and extreme lateral G-forces, the piston skirts can wear through the factory coating, causing vertical scoring in the cylinder walls (most commonly cylinders 4 and 8). This manifests as a distinct metallic ticking or knocking noise, excessive oil consumption, and misfires.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, the block can be machined and fitted with aftermarket Darton iron cylinder sleeves to permanently resolve the issue. If the scoring has damaged the pistons or connecting rods, a full rebuilt M178 short block or complete engine is required.

items.title: Hot-Vee Turbo Oil Line Coking and Leaks
items.whatHappens: By placing the twin turbochargers inside the "V" of the engine, AMG achieved incredible throttle response but created an extreme heat environment. The factory rubber and plastic turbo oil feed and return lines bake over time, leading to external oil leaks onto the hot exhaust (creating smoke and a fire risk) or internal coking that starves the turbo bearings of lubrication.
items.repairVsReplace: Upgrading to high-temperature silicone or braided stainless steel oil lines is a mandatory preventative measure for any M178 owner. If the turbos have already suffered bearing failure due to oil starvation, they must be rebuilt or replaced.

items.title: Dry-Sump Oil Pump Chain Stretch
items.whatHappens: The dry-sump system relies on a dedicated oil pump driven by a chain. Over time, this chain can stretch, or the tensioner can weaken, leading to a rattling noise from the front of the engine and potential drops in oil pressure during aggressive cornering or high-RPM use.
items.repairVsReplace: Replacing the oil pump chain and tensioner is a known, labour-intensive repair requiring front-end disassembly, but it is critical to prevent catastrophic oil starvation.

items.title: Intake Valve Carbon Buildup
items.whatHappens: As a direct injection engine, fuel does not wash over the back of the intake valves. Combined with the PCV system routing oil vapours into the intake tract, hard carbon deposits bake onto the valves, restricting airflow.
items.repairVsReplace: This causes rough idling, hesitation, and reduced power. The definitive repair is a professional "walnut blasting" service to clean the intake ports and valves.

failures.goodYearsLine: Post-2019 models feature revised piston skirt coatings, improved cylinder honing processes from the factory, and updated turbo oil line materials, significantly reducing the risk of cylinder scoring and making them the most robust examples of the M178 family .

variants.title: M178 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: ═══════════════════════════════════════ INTRO: The M178 family shares the same fundamental 4.0L DOHC "Hot-Vee" twin-turbo V8 block architecture and dry-sump lubrication, but power output, turbo sizing, and internal components vary significantly depending on the performance tier. Identifying your exact sub-code is mandatory, as fitting the wrong revision can lead to severe mechanical and ECU incompatibility. - Fitted to: AMG GT (C190), AMG GT S (C190) - Key technical difference: The base and mid-tier variants, featuring standard-sized twin turbochargers and a specific dry-sump calibration optimized for road and light track use. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; highly susceptible to cylinder scoring if driven hard on track days without adequate cool-down periods. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with higher-output variants due to different ECU mapping, turbo plumbing, and exhaust configurations. - Fitted to: AMG GT C (C190), AMG GT R (C190) - Key technical difference: The high-performance variant, featuring larger twin turbochargers, upgraded intercoolers, forged internal components, and an aggressive camshaft profile to deliver massive top-end power and track-focused thermal management. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; the higher continuous thermal and boost loads accelerate hot-vee oil line coking and turbo wear. - Interchange note: Requires matching high-flow turbos, specific ECU calibration, and upgraded cooling systems; not a direct drop-in for base GT models without extensive modification. - Fitted to: AMG GT Black Series (C192) - Key technical difference: The ultimate, track-homologated variant. Features flat-plane crankshaft technology (in specific markets/configurations), massively enlarged turbochargers, a revised dry-sump system with increased capacity, and extreme internal fortification. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; the extreme operating parameters demand meticulous, race-spec maintenance intervals. - Interchange note: Highly specialized; not interchangeable with any other M178 variant without a complete drivetrain and ECU overhaul.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement M178 Engine - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: Buying a used M178 engine carries extreme financial risk unless a professional borescope inspection of all eight cylinders has been performed to definitively rule out Alusil cylinder scoring. Given the £6,000+ cost of machining and sleeving a scored block, purchasing a used unit with unknown history or without verified bore health is highly discouraged.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned M178 engine is the sweet spot for most buyers. A reputable rebuild will proactively address the fatal Alusil scoring flaw by borescoping and installing Darton iron cylinder sleeves if necessary, upgrading the hot-vee turbo oil lines to high-temperature materials, performing a walnut blast carbon clean, and renewing all dry-sump seals.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full M178 engine rebuild is highly justified for track-day enthusiasts or collectors where maximum horsepower, reliability, and originality are required. An upgraded rebuild should include forged pistons, upgraded connecting rods, and precision-balanced rotating assemblies to handle well over 700 hp safely.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing and fitting through our vetted network ensures your M178 engine is installed by specialists equipped to handle the complex dry-sump plumbing, Hot-Vee layout, and AMG electronics, backed by a nationwide warranty.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: Because the M178 is found in modern AMG GT vehicles valued between £60,000 and £250,000+, a full engine replacement is a financially viable necessity to protect the asset's value. However, due to the high cost of the engine and the specialized labour required, always ensure the replacement cost is weighed against the vehicle's current market valuation .

items.question: How much does a Mercedes M178 engine replacement cost?
items.answer: A reconditioned Mercedes-AMG M178 engine typically costs between £8,000 and £12,000 for supply only . Fitted costs generally range from £10,500 to £15,000 depending on the specialist, while used units can be found from £5,000 but carry an extreme financial risk due to the high potential for Alusil cylinder wall scoring on track-driven examples. → Compare M178 engine replacement quotes today

items.question: What is the most common failure on the M178 engine?
items.answer: The most documented issues are cylinder wall scoring (Alusil block wear), hot-vee turbo oil line coking, and dry-sump oil pump chain stretch. Cylinder scoring causes metallic ticking and excessive oil consumption, while coked oil lines can starve the twin turbos of lubrication, leading to catastrophic bearing failure under high G-forces. → Get quotes for a rebuilt M178 with these issues resolved

items.question: Which Mercedes models use the M178 engine?
items.answer: The M178 is exclusively fitted to the AMG GT lineage (C190/C192 chassis), including the AMG GT, GT S, GT C, GT R, and GT Black Series, serving as the definitive mid-engine sports car powerplant from 2015 onwards. → Check your registration to confirm your exact M178 fitment

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned M178 engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned M178 is strongly recommended over a used unit. A proper rebuild will proactively address the fatal Alusil scoring flaw by installing Darton iron cylinder sleeves, upgrading the hot-vee oil lines to high-temperature materials, and renewing all dry-sump seals, whereas a used engine with unknown track history risks immediate, catastrophic bore failure. → Compare reconditioned M178 engine prices from UK specialists

items.question: What is the difference between M178.980, .985, and .990?
items.answer: The M178.980 is the base/mid-tier variant (GT/GT S) with standard turbos, the .985 is the high-performance variant (GT C/GT R) featuring larger turbos and forged internals, and the .990 is the ultimate track-homologated variant (GT Black Series) with extreme internal fortification and revised dry-sump capacity. They share the same core block, but the turbo plumbing, ECU mapping, and internal components differ significantly. → Enter your reg above to identify your exact M178 sub-code ═══════════════════════════════════════
